name: Oma Nkechi's Stitchwork Pullover
description:
Everyone in the Tier 2 Aboagye-Lindqvist neighborhood knows someone who has one of these. Nkechi Aboagye, who goes by Oma Nkechi to the block, has been knitting and selling pullovers from her apartment on the 14th floor of the Greaves stack for twenty-three years. The yarn is a blend she sources herself — recycled wool-analog, some real merino she trades favors for, occasionally a fiber that shifts color slightly with body heat that she picks up from a supplier she won't name. Each sweater has her signature asymmetrical ribbing at the hem and a different front panel motif — geometric, often Akan-derived, occasionally incorporating Nordic grid patterns from her late husband's family.

They are not cheap for the neighborhood — Φ65 to Φ90 depending on the yarn — but they last a decade of hard wear and she repairs them for free. Owning one marks you as someone who lives in or is connected to a specific few blocks of Tier 2 Chicago-North. It's a geographic and social belonging, knitted in.
what_it_says: You are from the neighborhood, or you were gifted in, or you found one secondhand and know enough to respect what it means. It is a warm sweater and a community credential.
worn_by: people given one as a gift
story_hooks: Oma Nkechi has started putting something inside the sweaters — a tiny folded note, a seed, something different each time — and no one knows why yet.
A Tier 5 fashion house has 'discovered' her work and wants to license the motifs; her community is split between wanting her to get paid and knowing what licensing actually means.
One specific sweater, a particular deep blue with a solar-cross motif, keeps appearing in the backgrounds of unrelated crime scenes across three months.
